title: Daodejing, chapter 21 (Mawangdui silk manuscripts)
language: Classical Chinese (silk transcription; received text) / English
source: Mawangdui Laozi A and B silk manuscripts (plates of Changsha Mawangdui Han mu jianbo jicheng vol. 1, via Wikimedia Commons) + Wikisource column transcription + Wang Bi received text (Wikisource) + Legge 1891 English (Project Gutenberg)
description: Daodejing chapter 21 as written on the two Mawangdui silk manuscripts of the Laozi (before 168 BCE), with Legge's English and the received Chinese text.
introduction:
Chapter 21 of the Daodejing (Laozi), shown on the two oldest nearly complete copies of the work: the silk manuscripts Laozi A and Laozi B, found in 1973 in Tomb 3 at Mawangdui, Changsha (Hunan), a tomb sealed in 168 BCE. Laozi A is written in a script between seal and clerical forms and does not avoid the personal name of the Han founder Liu Bang (邦); it is commonly dated before 195 BCE. Laozi B is in clerical script, avoids 邦, and is commonly dated 194-180 BCE. Both put the De part (chapters 38-81) before the Dao part (chapters 1-37), and a few chapters stand in a different order from the received text.

Each section gives the silk transcription column by column, with the Jicheng column number before each column (for Laozi B, 上 and 下 are the upper and lower halves of a column, photographed on facing plates), and links to the plate that carries those columns. □ marks a lost character; ∠, ‧ and ﹦ are marks written on the silk (﹦ repeats the character before it). Below the transcription is the received text of the Wang Bi recension, which is the text James Legge translated in 1891; the silk wording differs from it, most visibly in 恆 for received 常 (the received text avoids the name of Emperor Wen, Liu Heng), in the frequent final particle 也, and in loan characters such as 胃 for 謂.
translator_notes: English: James Legge, The Tao Teh King (Sacred Books of the East 39, 1891); Legge's paragraph numbers are kept as superscripts.
Legge translated the received text, not the silk manuscripts. Where the silk wording differs, his English follows the received text shown under the transcription.
Silk transcription: Wikisource Page transcriptions of the Jicheng plates (revisions of 18 October 2026, marked not yet proofread on Wikisource), checked against the plates for each chapter opening.

translation.original_ref: Daodejing 21; Mawangdui Laozi A (甲本) col. 132 to 134; Jicheng vol. 1 plate p. 101
translation.original_text:
132孔德之容唯道是從道之物唯望唯忽□□□
133呵中有象呵望呵忽呵中有物呵∠幽呵鳴呵中有請也∠其請甚真其中□□
134自今及古其名不去以順眾父∠吾何以知眾父之然以此∠
translation.edition_text: 孔德之容，惟道是從。道之為物，惟恍惟惚。惚兮恍兮，其中有象；恍兮惚兮，其中有物。窈兮冥兮，其中有精；其精甚真，其中有信。自今及古，其名不去，以閱眾甫。吾何以知眾甫之狀哉？以此。
translation.text:
The grandest forms of active force
From Tao come, their only source.
Who can of Tao the nature tell?
Our sight it flies, our touch as well.
Eluding sight, eluding touch,
The forms of things all in it crouch;
Eluding touch, eluding sight,
There are their semblances, all right.
Profound it is, dark and obscure;
Things' essences all there endure.
Those essences the truth enfold
Of what, when seen, shall then be told.
Now it is so; 'twas so of old.
Its name--what passes not away;
So, in their beautiful array,
Things form and never know decay.

How know I that it is so with all the beauties of existing things? By this (nature of the Tao).
translation.scan_note: Laozi A (甲本), columns 132 to 134, on plate p. 101 of Changsha Mawangdui Han mu jianbo jicheng, vol. 1 (column numbers are printed under each plate; the columns run from right to left). Checked on the image: column 132 reads 而貴食母 孔德之容 (the opening of this chapter, with the end of the preceding text where shown). □ marks a character lost on the silk (5 in this section). Transcription and column numbers: Wikisource 老子 (帛書甲本), which follows the Jicheng column numbering. The English is Legge's translation of the received text, shown below the silk transcription; the silk wording differs from it in many places, so compare the two Chinese texts for the variants.
